Rivers are the planet's great storytellers. Each one starts small, as snowmelt trickling off a mountain, a spring bubbling up through limestone, or rain gathering in a mossy hollow. Those threads of water join and grow until they carve valleys, shape continents, and set the course of human history.

For as long as there have been people, there have been people living beside rivers. The Nile's yearly floods left rich silt on its banks, and Egyptian civilization grew out of that soil. The Tigris and Euphrates watered Mesopotamia, where writing, law, and cities first appeared. The Indus, the Yellow River, and the Ganges each supported cultures whose influence lasts today. Rivers gave people drinking water, fish, fertile farmland, and, above all, a way to travel. Before roads and railways, a river was a highway that carried goods, ideas, and armies.

Rivers are also living systems. A healthy river supports a web of life that runs from microscopic algae to salmon swimming thousands of miles upstream to spawn where they hatched. Wetlands along riverbanks filter pollutants, soak up floodwater, and shelter migrating birds. Even the sediment a river carries matters, because it builds deltas, feeds coastal marshes, and replenishes beaches.

A river's character changes along its length. Near the source it tends to be fast, cold, and narrow, rushing over rocks and dropping down waterfalls. Downstream it slows and widens, curving through meanders and oxbow lakes until it reaches the sea.

Today many rivers are under strain. Dams break up habitats, pollution fouls the water, and climate change shifts rainfall and shrinks glaciers. Yet restoration efforts show that rivers can recover when given the chance. Removing dams has brought fish back within a few years, and cleanup campaigns have revived waterways once written off as dead.

A river is always moving and changing but still recognizably itself, a reminder that water connects everything.
